summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights and held that Rule 78.07(c) applies to termination cases, so complaints about the form of the judgment or about missing statutorily required findings are not preserved unless first raised in a motion to amend the judgment.
key_cases.relevance: This decision controls whether a parent can obtain reversal for omitted statutory findings, and it is the single most common preservation trap in Missouri child-welfare appeals.
key_cases.quote: Every district of the court of appeals has held, and this Court agrees, that Rule 78.07(c) applies to termination of parental rights cases.

key_cases.case_name: Sercl v. Director, Department of Social Services, Children's Division
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for the alleged perpetrator, holding that the Division bears the burden to prove neglect by a preponderance of the evidence before a name may be placed on the Central Registry and that a judgment against the party with the burden need not be supported by substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Sercl is a working example of a court setting aside an agency substantiation because the agency's evidence did not carry its burden.
key_cases.quote: assign to the Division the burden to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Sercl neglected K.J. by failing to provide her with the care necessary for her well-being

key_cases.case_name: C.D.J., Jr. v. Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that a family whose child is recorded as abused has standing to seek review and that the Children's Division lacks statutory authority to substantiate a report of abuse by an 'unknown perpetrator.'
key_cases.relevance: The case is an example of a court invalidating an agency finding that exceeded the agency's statutory authority.
key_cases.quote: the Children's Division does not have the statutory authority to substantiate a report that an "unknown perpetrator" committed child abuse

key_cases.case_name: Greene County Juvenile Office v. K.J.C.
key_cases.holding: The court reversed, holding that the evidence did not clearly and convincingly show the children were without proper care, custody or support, so the juvenile court erred in taking jurisdiction and removing them from an arguably over-protective but not abusive mother.
key_cases.relevance: This is Missouri's clearest recent published reversal of a juvenile court's assumption of jurisdiction over children for want of evidence.
key_cases.quote: the trial court must find by clear and convincing evidence that the child is without proper care, custody, or support

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma v. Sifferman
key_cases.holding: On the Choctaw Nation's petition, the court made its writ of prohibition permanent, holding that the juvenile court had no express or implied authority to intervene in the Children's Division's internal administrative review of a non-final adoption recommendation or to compel a particular recommendation.
key_cases.relevance: This is an example of an appellate court vacating a juvenile court's order for exceeding the court's statutory authority over an agency's internal process.
key_cases.quote: Respondent did not have the express or implied authority to interfere in the Children's Division's administrative review of a nonfinal administrative recommendation for adoption

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of the mother's parental rights and remanded, holding that past acts support termination only when convincingly linked to predicted future harm, that findings supporting the earlier assumption of jurisdiction must be updated to describe the parent's condition at the time of the termination hearing, and that the trial court's findings here were insufficient on every ground relied on.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Missouri Supreme Court reversing a termination outright for findings that recycled the jurisdictional record instead of describing the parent at the time of trial — the strongest reversal authority a Missouri parent has.
key_cases.quote: To that end, a trial court cannot support a termination by merely incorporating earlier findings supporting its assumption of jurisdiction or some other earlier disposition.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of an incarcerated immigrant mother's parental rights and the grant of adoption to the private petitioners, holding it was plain error resulting in manifest injustice to enter judgment without the investigations and written reports mandated by sections 211.455, 453.070 and 453.077, and remanded for those reports and a new trial.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Missouri Supreme Court vacating a completed termination and adoption because the mandatory investigation and reporting steps were skipped, and it shows that such statutory omissions can be reached as plain error even when unpreserved.
key_cases.quote: In this case, the complete failure to comply with the mandatory provisions of sections 453.070 and 453.077 requires that the judgment be reversed.

state_agency.name: Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division

timeline_requirements.deadline: 30 days to file a petition for direct judicial review with the circuit court as provided in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 536.100; choosing this route waives administrative review, and on service of the petition the division lists the alleged perpetrator's name in the central registry pending further orders or judgment of the circuit court
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the notification of the division's preliminary (preponderance of the evidence) finding of child abuse or neglect

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days to request administrative review by the Child Abuse and Neglect Review Board in writing; mutually exclusive with direct judicial review, and the alleged perpetrator is not listed in the central registry for that finding unless and until the board sustains it. Where criminal charges arising out of the facts of the investigation are pending, 60 days from the court's final disposition or dismissal of the charges
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: If the division does not receive a request for administrative review within 60 days of notification of the preliminary finding, it lists the alleged perpetrator as a perpetrator of child abuse or neglect in the central registry (13 CSR 35-31.025(3)(B)1.C)

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Judicial review of review board decision
timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days to request de novo judicial review in the circuit court of the county in which the alleged perpetrator resides, or in Cole County
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notification of the decision of the Child Abuse and Neglect Review Board
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 210.152.6
